title: Series & Parallel Networks
description: Collapse resistor networks to find equivalent resistances, branch currents, voltages and powers.

study.title: Series or parallel?
study.body: Two elements are in **series** when they share a node that nothing else touches: they carry the same current. Two elements are in **parallel** when both ends connect to the same pair of nodes: they have the same voltage. Label every node first; elements that touch the same two labels are in parallel.
study.formula: R_s = R_1 + R_2 \qquad R_p = \frac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2}

study.title: Strategy: collapse, then expand
study.body: Combine resistors starting at the end farthest from the source until one $R_{eq}$ is left, and find the source current $I = V_s/R_{eq}$. Then expand back: Ohm's law and dividers give every branch. Here: $R_2 \parallel R_3$ = 2 kΩ, $R_{eq}$ = 3 kΩ, $I$ = 4 mA, so $v_x$ = 8 V and each 4 kΩ resistor carries 2 mA.

study.title: Shortcuts
study.body: The voltage divider splits a voltage over series resistors; the current divider splits a current over two parallel resistors (note: the **other** resistor goes on top). $n$ equal resistors $R$ in parallel give $R/n$. A parallel combination is always smaller than its smallest member, a quick sanity check.

study.title: Common mistakes
study.body:
- Calling two resistors 'in series' while a third branch leaves the node between them.
- Missing a wire drawn across a resistor: that resistor is shorted, carries no current and drops out.
- Putting the wrong resistor on top in the current divider.
- Forgetting that $R_{ab}$ depends on which two terminals you look into: a branch that ends on an open terminal carries no current.

steps.prompt: All values are shown in the schematic.

ask.prompt: Find the equivalent resistance seen by the source.
ask.explanation: $R_2 \parallel R_3$ = {{par(R2,R3)|Ω}} is in series with $R_1$: $R_{eq}$ = {{R1|Ω}} + {{par(R2,R3)|Ω}} = **{{Vs/I_Vs|Ω}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the current supplied by the source.

ask.explanation: With $R_p = R_2 \parallel R_3$ = {{par(R2,R3)|Ω}} the divider gives $V_{R_3} = V_s\frac{R_p}{R_1+R_p}$ = {{Vs|V}} · {{par(R2,R3)/(R1+par(R2,R3))||3}} = **{{abs(V_R3)|V}}**.
$R_2$ and $R_3$ are in parallel, so both have $V_x = V_s\frac{R_p}{R_1+R_p}$ = {{abs(V_R3)|V}} with $R_p$ = {{par(R2,R3)|Ω}}. Then $I_{R_2}$ = {{abs(V_R3)|V}} / {{R2|Ω}} = **{{abs(I_R2)|A}}**.

steps.prompt: Which statement about this network is true?
options: $R_3$ and $R_4$ are in series, and that pair is in parallel with $R_2$
steps.explanation: $R_3$ and $R_4$ share a node that nothing else touches, so they are in series. The pair runs from node $x$ to ground, just like $R_2$, so $R_2 \parallel (R_3 + R_4)$. $R_1$ and $R_2$ are **not** in series: the $R_3$ branch leaves the node between them. $R_3$ alone is not parallel to $R_2$ because its lower end is not at ground.

steps.prompt: All values are shown in the schematic.

ask.prompt: Find the equivalent resistance seen by the source.
ask.explanation: $R_3 + R_4$ = {{R3+R4|Ω}}; in parallel with $R_2$: {{par(R2,R3+R4)|Ω}}; plus $R_1$: $R_{eq}$ = **{{Vs/I_Vs|Ω}}**.

$R_p = R_2 \parallel (R_3+R_4)$ = {{par(R2,R3+R4)|Ω}}, so $v_x = V_s\frac{R_p}{R_1+R_p}$ = {{par(R2,R3+R4)*Vs/(R1+par(R2,R3+R4))|V}}. Divide $v_x$ over $R_3$ and $R_4$: $V_{R_4} = v_x\frac{R_4}{R_3+R_4}$ = **{{abs(V_R4)|V}}**.
$v_x = V_s\frac{R_p}{R_1+R_p}$ with $R_p = R_2 \parallel (R_3+R_4)$ = {{par(R2,R3+R4)|Ω}}, so $v_x$ = {{abs(V_R2)|V}} and $I_{R_2} = v_x/R_2$ = **{{abs(I_R2)|A}}**.
The source current flows through $R_1$: $I = V_s/R_{eq}$ = {{Vs|V}} / {{R1+par(R2,R3+R4)|Ω}} = {{I_Vs|A}}. Then $P = I^2R_1$ = **{{P_R1|W}}**.

steps.prompt: A current source drives the network; values are in the schematic.

ask.prompt: Find the voltage across the current source.
ask.explanation: The source sees $R_1 \parallel (R_2+R_3)$ = {{par(R1,R2+R3)|Ω}}, so $V = I_s R$ = {{Is|A}} · {{par(R1,R2+R3)|Ω}} = **{{V_Is|V}}**.
Current divider between $R_1$ and the branch $R_2+R_3$ = {{R2+R3|Ω}}: $I_{R_3} = I_s\frac{R_1}{R_1+R_2+R_3}$ = **{{abs(I_R3)|A}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the power delivered by the current source.
ask.explanation: $P = I_s^2 R_{eq}$ with $R_{eq} = R_1 \parallel (R_2+R_3)$ = {{par(R1,R2+R3)|Ω}}: $P$ = **{{P_Is|W}}**.

steps.prompt: If $R_3$ in this circuit is replaced by a short circuit, $R_2$ carries no current.
steps.explanation: A short across $R_3$ also connects the top of $R_2$ to ground, so $R_2$ has 0 V across it and carries no current. All of the source current then flows through $R_1$ and the short: $I = V_s/R_1$.

steps.prompt: The network has three terminals; the third terminal is left open each time.

ask.prompt: Find the resistance $R_{ab}$ between terminals a and b.
ask.explanation: With c open, $R_3$ and $R_4$ are in series ({{R3+R4|Ω}}), and that path is parallel to $R_2$ between node x and b: {{par(R2,R3+R4)|Ω}}. Add $R_1$: $R_{ab}$ = **{{R_a_b|Ω}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the resistance $R_{ac}$ between terminals a and c.
ask.explanation: With b open, $R_2$ and $R_4$ are in series ({{R2+R4|Ω}}) and parallel to $R_3$: {{par(R3,R2+R4)|Ω}}. Add $R_1$: $R_{ac}$ = **{{R_a_c|Ω}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the resistance $R_{bc}$ between terminals b and c.
ask.explanation: With a open, $R_1$ carries no current. Between b and c: $R_4 \parallel (R_2+R_3)$ = {{R4|Ω}} ∥ {{R2+R3|Ω}} = **{{R_b_c|Ω}}**.

steps.hint: A resistor that ends on an open terminal carries no current.

steps.prompt: All values are shown in the schematic.

ask.prompt: Find the current supplied by the source.

ask.explanation: $R_p$ = {{par(R2+R3,R4+R5)|Ω}} gives $v_x = V_s\frac{R_p}{R_1+R_p}$ = {{abs(V_R4+V_R5)|V}}. Divide over the right branch: $V_{R_5} = v_x\frac{R_5}{R_4+R_5}$ = **{{abs(V_R5)|V}}**.
$v_x = V_s\frac{R_p}{R_1+R_p}$ = {{abs(V_R2+V_R3)|V}} with $R_p$ = {{par(R2+R3,R4+R5)|Ω}}. The left branch carries $v_x/(R_2+R_3)$ = {{abs(V_R2+V_R3)|V}} / {{R2+R3|Ω}} = **{{abs(I_R3)|A}}**.
$R_1$ carries the full source current $I = V_s/R_{eq}$ = {{I_Vs|A}} ($R_{eq}$ = {{R1+par(R2+R3,R4+R5)|Ω}}), so $P = I^2R_1$ = **{{P_R1|W}}**.

steps.prompt: A current source feeds $R_1$ and three parallel resistors.

ask.explanation: $R_1$ is in series with the source, so it carries exactly $I_s$: $V_{R_1} = I_sR_1$ = {{Is|A}} · {{R1|Ω}} = **{{abs(V_R1)|V}}**.
$R_2 \parallel R_3 \parallel R_4$ = {{par(R2,R3,R4)|Ω}}, so $v_x = I_s R_p$ = {{Is*par(R2,R3,R4)|V}} and $I_{R_3} = v_x/R_3$ = **{{abs(I_R3)|A}}**. $R_1$ does not matter here.

ask.prompt: Find the voltage across the current source.
ask.explanation: $V = I_s(R_1 + R_2 \parallel R_3 \parallel R_4)$ = {{Is|A}} · ({{R1|Ω}} + {{par(R2,R3,R4)|Ω}}) = **{{V_Is|V}}**.

steps.prompt: In this circuit, increasing $R_1$ changes the current through $R_3$.
steps.explanation: $R_1$ is in series with an ideal current source, so the current into node x is $I_s$ whatever $R_1$ is. The split over $R_2$, $R_3$, $R_4$ is unchanged; only the voltage across the source grows.

steps.prompt: Look carefully at every wire. Tap every resistor that carries **no current**.
steps.explanation:
A resistor with a plain wire across it has both ends on the same node, so $v = 0$ and $i = 0$.
- $R_6$ is bridged by the wire on the far right.
- $R_7$ is bridged by the wire drawn below it.
With those two out of the way the network is $R_1 + R_2 \parallel (R_3 + R_4 \parallel R_5)$: $R_5$ now runs from the top node straight to the bottom rail, in parallel with $R_4$.

steps.prompt: Three-terminal network; the third terminal is left open each time.

ask.explanation: With c open, $R_4$ and $R_5$ form one series path (via the bottom wire) from x to y: {{R4+R5|Ω}}, parallel to $R_2$: {{par(R2,R4+R5)|Ω}}. Then $R_{ab} = R_1 + R_2\parallel(R_4+R_5) + R_3$ = **{{R_a_b|Ω}}**.
With b open, $R_3$ carries no current. From x to c: $R_4 \parallel (R_2+R_5)$ = {{par(R4,R2+R5)|Ω}}. Add $R_1$: $R_{ac}$ = **{{R_a_c|Ω}}**.
With a open, $R_1$ carries no current. From y to c: $R_5 \parallel (R_2+R_4)$ = {{par(R5,R2+R4)|Ω}}. Add $R_3$: $R_{bc}$ = **{{R_b_c|Ω}}**.

steps.prompt: All values are shown in the schematic.

ask.explanation: $R_1$ sits directly across the source, so $I_{R_1} = V_s/R_1$ = {{Vs|V}} / {{R1|Ω}} = **{{abs(I_R1)|A}}**. The other branch does not affect it.

ask.prompt: Find the current supplied by the source.
ask.explanation: Branch 1: $V_s/R_1$ = {{Vs/R1|A}}. Branch 2: $V_s/(R_2 + R_3\parallel R_4)$ = {{Vs|V}} / {{R2+par(R3,R4)|Ω}} = {{Vs/(R2+par(R3,R4))|A}}. KCL: $I$ = **{{I_Vs|A}}**.
The right branch has the full $V_s$ across it. Divider: $V_{R_4} = V_s\frac{R_3\parallel R_4}{R_2 + R_3\parallel R_4}$ = {{Vs|V}} · {{par(R3,R4)|Ω}} / {{R2+par(R3,R4)|Ω}} = **{{abs(V_R4)|V}}**.
Branch current $I_2 = V_s/(R_2 + R_3\parallel R_4)$ = {{abs(I_R2)|A}}, so $P = I_2^2R_2$ = **{{P_R2|W}}**.

steps.prompt: Put the steps for finding one branch current in a series-parallel network in order.
items: Label the nodes and spot series and parallel groups
Combine the groups step by step into $R_{eq}$
Work back toward the branch with Ohm's law and dividers
steps.explanation: Collapse the network to a single resistance to get the source current, then expand it again in the reverse order, using the voltage or current divider at each split until you reach the branch you need.

steps.prompt: Six resistors, one source. All values are shown in the schematic.

ask.prompt: Find the equivalent resistance seen by the source.
ask.explanation: Three parallel branches: {{R2+R3|Ω}}, {{R4|Ω}} and {{R5+R6|Ω}}, together {{par(R2+R3,R4,R5+R6)|Ω}}. Add $R_1$: $R_{eq}$ = **{{Vs/I_Vs|Ω}}**.
$R_p = (R_2+R_3)\parallel R_4 \parallel (R_5+R_6)$ = {{par(R2+R3,R4,R5+R6)|Ω}}, so $v_x = V_s\frac{R_p}{R_1+R_p}$ = {{abs(V_R4)|V}}. Then $V_{R_6} = v_x\frac{R_6}{R_5+R_6}$ = **{{abs(V_R6)|V}}**.
$v_x$ = {{abs(V_R4)|V}} (as above). The left branch carries $v_x/(R_2+R_3)$ = {{abs(I_R2)|A}}, so $P = I^2R_2$ = **{{P_R2|W}}**.

steps.prompt: Look carefully at every wire before you start.

ask.prompt: Find the equivalent resistance seen by the source.
ask.explanation: The wire drawn over $R_2$ shorts it: both ends are the same node, so it drops out. What is left: $R_1 + R_3\parallel R_4$ = {{R1|Ω}} + {{par(R3,R4)|Ω}} = **{{Vs/I_Vs|Ω}}**.
$R_2$ is shorted by the wire above it. Divider: $V_{R_4} = V_s\frac{R_3\parallel R_4}{R_1 + R_3\parallel R_4}$ = {{Vs|V}} · {{par(R3,R4)|Ω}} / {{R1+par(R3,R4)|Ω}} = **{{abs(V_R4)|V}}**.
With $R_2$ shorted, $v_x = V_s\frac{R_3\parallel R_4}{R_1+R_3\parallel R_4}$ = {{abs(V_R3)|V}}, so $I_{R_3} = v_x/R_3$ = **{{abs(I_R3)|A}}**.

steps.hint: Is there a resistor with both ends on the same node?

steps.prompt: In this six-resistor network, which statement is true?
options: $R_4$ is in parallel with the series pair $R_5$, $R_6$
steps.explanation: $R_4$ runs from node x to the bottom rail, and so does the path $R_5$–$R_6$ (whose middle node touches nothing else): they are in parallel. $R_2$ alone is not parallel to $R_4$; only the pair $R_2 + R_3$ is. $R_1$ is not in series with $R_4$ because three branches leave node x.

steps.prompt: A current source drives five resistors.

ask.prompt: Find the voltage across the current source.
ask.explanation: From the far end: $R_3+R_4$ = {{R3+R4|Ω}}, parallel $R_5$: {{par(R3+R4,R5)|Ω}}, plus $R_2$: {{R2+par(R3+R4,R5)|Ω}}, parallel $R_1$: {{par(R1,R2+par(R3+R4,R5))|Ω}}. $V = I_sR_{eq}$ = **{{V_Is|V}}**.

Current divider at the source: the $R_2$ branch ({{R2+par(R3+R4,R5)|Ω}}) gets $I_s\frac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2 + (R_3+R_4)\parallel R_5}$ = {{abs(I_R2)|A}}. Divide again: $I_{R_5} = I_{R_2}\frac{R_3+R_4}{R_3+R_4+R_5}$ = **{{abs(I_R5)|A}}**.

ask.prompt: What percentage of the source power is absorbed by $R_1$?
ask.explanation: $R_1$ is directly across the source, so $P_{R_1} = V^2/R_1$ with $V$ = {{V_Is|V}}: {{P_R1|W}}. The source delivers $P = VI_s$ = {{P_Is|W}}. Ratio: **{{100*P_R1/P_Is|%}}**.

steps.prompt: If every resistor in a network driven by a single voltage source is doubled, the source current halves.
steps.explanation: Doubling every resistor doubles $R_{eq}$, and $I = V_s/R_{eq}$. All voltage-divider ratios stay the same, so every resistor voltage is unchanged while every current halves.

steps.prompt: Three-terminal network; the third terminal is left open each time.

ask.explanation: With c open, $R_4$ is dangling. Between x and b: $R_2 \parallel (R_3+R_5)$ = {{par(R2,R3+R5)|Ω}}. Add $R_1$: $R_{ab}$ = **{{R_a_b|Ω}}**.
With b open: from x to y, $R_3 \parallel (R_2+R_5)$ = {{par(R3,R2+R5)|Ω}}. Then $R_{ac} = R_1 + $ {{par(R3,R2+R5)|Ω}} $+ R_4$ = **{{R_a_c|Ω}}**.
With a open, $R_1$ is dangling. From b to y: $R_5 \parallel (R_2+R_3)$ = {{par(R5,R2+R3)|Ω}}; add $R_4$: $R_{bc}$ = **{{R_b_c|Ω}}**.
